utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-97-25-T, the Prosecutor versus Milorad Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Judge Mumba, as the Vice-President of the Tribunal, has other authorised Tribunal business this morning which was unavoidable, unfortunately, so she will not be here and we are proceeding in accordance with Rule 15 bis of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Now, Mr. Bakrac, you are cross-examining.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Bakrac: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Taranin.

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will continue from where we broke off yesterday. In your answers to the Prosecutor's questions you spoke about food as well. You mentioned that you got bread and some kind of soup. However, in the statements you gave to the investigators of the OTP, you said that for breakfast sometimes you got eggs, that you got beans, rice, potatoes, pasta; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was some of that, but that was at a late stage and we got that only for about 15 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. As for hygiene, is it correct that you said to the investigators of the OTP that at the very outset until the autumn, the hygienic conditions were not bad, that after that the pipes froze and also the central heating system went down when the boiler broke; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for hygiene, our accommodation was normal, but we could not use the bathrooms or anything. We could not take baths. I said that probably the boiler room was broken, so we could not take baths and there was no water in the pipes, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what I read from your statement is correct?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you heard what I said to you just now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Also in the statement that you gave to the investigators of the OTP, you mentioned 11 persons who, when the International Red Cross came to the KP Dom, were at the bakery. Were those persons brought in and were they registered on that day by the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: These 11 persons were walking towards the bakery and they were put up somewhere there. I could not see this when the International Red Cross -- however, when my brother, who was in that group, told me about it, or rather somebody's brother who was in that group told me about it, and then they were registered at their request. Unfortunately, some of those persons who were registered, although they were registered, are still missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly: They were registered on that day when the International Red Cross came?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They hid them. They hid them, but this brother of his -- remember, I told you that had to tell the International Red Cross that these 11 people were being hidden.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is whether they were registered later during the course of that same day.

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was not there, so I cannot tell you for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did the delegation of the International Red Cross stay at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see any. The first one, actually, I saw was at the very beginning of the war. How should I put this? The 29th or 30th. That's when the first International Red Cross came. And we were really surprised. I managed to register among five of them. Later on they didn't come again. Perhaps in a few months they came again, but then I never saw them again after that, because I did different things, including in the kitchen, so I never saw them again. They never called me to come in again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am going to read your sentence. "These 11 persons were returned to the detention facilities and were registered."

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, possibly, but I did not see this, so I can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, just wait for the pause at the end of the question before you start the answer. The translators were well behind you there. Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would just like to clarify something. You mentioned the 29th, 30th. Which month is this?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the year?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday in your statement, you mentioned Mr. Starovic, Koprivica, and Vladicic, interrogators of the KP Dom. You said that you knew that he worked earlier on at the MUP as an inspector, too. Do you know what the other two, Starovic and Koprivica, did before the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not very familiar with that, but I know about Vladicic because we were great friends; we were colleagues when it was necessary. He worked at the SUP as an inspector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I could not recognise Koprivica immediately, but he made it known to me that I knew him and that he knew me. Later on I figured it out. But I knew Starovic, Starovic is the brother-in-law or son-in-law of my director, Mr. Stankovic, so I knew him well, but then I didn't know where he exactly worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With the permission of the Court, I'm going to ask you once again to hear out what I have to ask, and then wait for it to be fully interpreted, and then answer, please. When you saw the mentioned three men, what were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly. I'm not sure whether they were in uniform or not, I don't know. I was afraid, so I wasn't all that careful because all of this took place within one minute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you also mentioned that you did not watch people being brought in and taken away and that you were afraid of hearing the beatings. Were there other persons in your room who did not watch this, who did not listen to this, and can you mention who are these persons from your room, because you spent time together and I'm sure you talked.

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people from my room who did watch, Kumor, who's in France today, was taken out of the KP Dom early; he was taken away by a man. And he listened the most, and he wanted to tell us about it, how he heard the moans and the screams, and we wouldn't allow him. Especially Husein Lojo, who is a professor, did not want him to tell us about this because he listened to all of this. Kumor Safet is his name. If he were to come here, he could tell you the best about all of this that went on because he listened the most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, Kumor Safet is the person who listened and watched and told the rest of you about this?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he could see anything, but he did listen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Look, sir, I know it's difficult, and I know you want to give your answer, but you are not giving that pause. Do you have the transcript coming up on your screen there in front of you? If you just wait till you see the typing finish you'll realise that the translation is also finishing, so wait for the typing to stop before you answer. Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. And I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Kumor Safet is the one who listened. Can you tell me which room you were in, and who was with you in that room?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the room with me there were six men in one small room with seven beds, Room 15. Lojo was with me, Husein Lojo; his brother; Tajko Tafro; Crneta, a forestry technician; Causevic, I don't know his first name exactly; Safet Kumor; and I was there as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you also said that in front of the KP Dom on the banks of the River Drina there was a dump where garbage was thrown. Is that near the bridge?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not far away from the bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was garbage thrown from the bridge as well?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It would be hard to throw from the bridge because you cannot have freight vehicles, trucks, coming onto the bridge for that purpose because it's a very narrow bridge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your claim that freight trucks cannot cross that bridge?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could not at that time because it was smaller, and also it was dangerous, so only small cars were allowed to pass.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How come you know that if you were detained at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lived in Foca for a long time. I was born in Foca. Perhaps you don't know that, or perhaps you don't know the geography of the town of Foca. You're pretending not to know it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is to say that before the conflict broke out, military trucks could not cross that bridge?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what they did during the war. Perhaps they expanded the bridge or enhanced it in some way, I don't know, during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday when you said that you were called to come to the administrative building, you said that you had to take off your white cap and white uniform. Why did you wear it?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say white coat, I said white cap.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do apologise. I understood that you also had a white coat. Perhaps I made a mistake, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you wear a white cap?

utterances.speaker: RASIM TARANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of hygiene, so that my hair would not fall into something. That's what my boss, Krsto Krnojelac, told me to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Re-examination, Ms. Kuo?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for giving evidence. You may leave now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too. And I do apologise if I did something wrong, if I offended someone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We understand entirely, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your understanding. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, are you taking the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It might have arrived at the time where we should suggest to the Prosecution that they spend more effort on the specific incidents which have been pleaded and less upon the general matters. We've had a lot of evidence now about such things as the crowded conditions at particular periods, the lack of food, the difficulties with hygiene, the lack of medical care in a general sense, beatings in a general sense, the labour; and with all due respect, despite the cross-examination this morning, I don't see that those are really in any dispute. The evidence about the outbreak of the conflict in Foca, nothing has been put to suggest that there wasn't a conflict. We are not concerned with who was responsible for starting it. The issue that has been raised as to whether the Muslims were also armed, well, there can be an armed conflict from both sides. Nobody is suggesting that we have to determine whether that was right or wrong. So could we get back to what's actually in the indictment, the pleaded incidents? We've got a number of beatings that are pleaded in the indictment which haven't been dealt with or which you may want to give some evidence, some supporting evidence on. Labour on the accused's house is an issue which can be dealt with more fully, certainly any particular medical incidents that have been pleaded. But otherwise we have amassing a huge amount of evidence which is not really in dispute about a lot of these issues. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think that's the general approach that we're beginning to adopt now that the pattern evidence seems to have been established reasonably well, and I will concentrate on those particular incidents that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If anything is really disputed by the accused, then you may certainly deal with that in as much detail as you need. But if something arises during the course of the Defence case where an issue is really disputed for the first time, then you have automatically, really, a case in reply on it. And I'm sure from the way in which Defence counsel have conducted themselves in this case, they realise that they have to dispute what is in dispute during the course of the cross-examination, and they appear to have done so with, I'm glad to say, careful economy, for which we are grateful. But we are, I think, getting to the stage where we can say the general matters, you have enough evidence. If that's the best you can do, you've done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's the general approach I'll adopt today and hopefully it will be as efficient as it can be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this witness has protective measures, a pseudonym and facial distortion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. And I've also placed on the pseudonym page in front of him just a couple of place names which may assist in the identification of who he is, so I might just refer to them briefly by a pseudonym as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. Well, this document, which is headed FWS-08, with the various pseudonyms and place names, will be Exhibit P408 and it will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And I think, Your Honour, the only pseudonym that in fact will be used will be a pseudonym A in relation to geography. The rest should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Has somebody explained to the witness that he should keep a careful watch on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: We've discussed a couple of approaches, and he hasn't -- he's not aware today whether or not we were going to go into closed session or in fact have an approach like this, but I'll briefly explain it to him when he arrives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There's been no suggestion of a closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No. Right. Well, may we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Will you please make the solemn declaration. It's on the card that's been handed to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'll just ask that Exhibit P408 be placed in front of the witness. Examined by Mr. Smith:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. In front of you is a piece of paper, Exhibit P408, with a name and date of birth at the top of it. Are they your personal details?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes, and they're correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And below that you'll see a couple of place names with letters alongside of them. Particularly in relation to the first place name, when I ask you questions that would relate to that place, could you use the letter A, as it's listed on the paper.

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also at the base of that page there's some other names with some corresponding numbers. If you'd like to refer to those people in your testimony, could you try and remember to use those numbers. I'll try and remind you as well.

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In April 1992 you lived in town A with your wife and children; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're a Bosnian Muslim by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were a manager of a business at that time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you a member of any political party in 1992?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of any military unit?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in April 1992 did you leave your hometown, that's town A, with your family?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you leave that town? Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: In principle, I'm a pacifist. I did not believe that everything that did happen would happen. When I finally realised what would happen, I wanted to get my family out. They could not take everything in town A, everything that was going on in town A, where we should have stayed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And briefly, what was going on in town A that made you want to leave?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: People were buying food, and I didn't do that. When I realised that I had to buy food for my family, it was too late and there was nowhere to buy it. Roadblocks were being set around town. It became increasingly difficult to get out of town, and I practically left, together with my family, at the very last moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you concerned about violence occurring in the area?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes, I was concerned. There were many people who were armed and I learned about a lot of things that happened around (redacted). There were a lot of barricades. Also it became more difficult for people to get in and out of town A.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you go to village B that night -- sorry, on one night in April did you travel to village B?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes. I went with my family to village B.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in village B?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: About a month and a half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 25th of May, 1992, about six weeks later, were you arrested by Montenegrin police?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you taken to the (redacted) police station?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else was with you when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: With me was Enes Bico and Bogosav Droca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were the three of you doing when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: At that moment we were driving in a car from town A to town C -- sorry, from town B to town C. We were stopped by the Montenegrin police and they asked us for documents. After that they said that we had to come with them to town C, to the police station, to make a statement. So that's how we got to town C, to the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the police station, was there anyone else detained there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes. There were many people who had been detained and who were kept in isolation cells, where they put us too; that is, myself and Enes Bico and Bogosav Droca was allowed to go. Although they were also arresting at the time people of Serb ethnicity, but my friend Bogosav Droca was an invalid. He did not have his right hand, and so that was probably the reason why they released him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you released from the police station?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you told why you were detained at the police station?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: No. We were told nothing. They simply put us in an isolation cell, where there were very many people already. And we were all crowded, packed like sardines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how many other detainees were there when you arrived at the police station?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: In my cell there were between 10 and 15 inmates. And the cells were very small, perhaps 2.5 times 2.5 or perhaps not more than 3 times 3. But there were also other cells, and they were full too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what ethnicity these people were? Were they one particular ethnicity, or were they a range?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Members of only one ethnic group were in those cells. In my cell, there were only Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you kept in that police station?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I was arrested around 8.00 in the morning, and in that isolation cell I was until about 4.00 in the afternoon when two buses came, picked up old people from police stations, and transported us to Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how many people were transported to Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I know for a fact that there were 22 Muslims then, but I do not know how many Serbs there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of these 22 Muslims, do you know whether they were soldiers or civilians at the time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Civilians, all of them, who were in different towns and had been picked up from streets or on highways.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know some of the towns in which they were -- which they came from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I do. It was practically the whole Montenegrin Riviera, Ulciny, Bar, Herceg-Novi, these -- Igalo near Herceg-Novi, these are principally the towns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you taken to the KP Dom in Foca that day?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes. That evening, we reached Foca at 10.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who took you there? Was it the (redacted) police, or was it someone else?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Policemen from (redacted) escorted us to a small locality called Pluzine. Other buses from Foca came to Pluzine, those that belonged to Focatrans hauler, and they were taken over by policemen from Foca, that is, from the KP Dom, who then took us to the penitentiary in Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told why you were being taken to KP Dom at any stage before you left the police station or any stage en route?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: No, we were told nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you passed, as you passed through the town of Foca, did you notice anything unusual as you approached the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I did. There were big bonfires. It was the 25th of May, and at first I thought they were proper bonfires because we used to mark that day once, but later on I realised that it was houses that were on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened when you first arrived at the KP Dom? Who were you handed over to?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: It was dark, there were no lights, and they took us off the bus, lined us up along the outside wall of the KP Dom, told us to put our hands up, and not to do anything stupid or else they will shoot. Behind us were men armed with automatic weapons. They frisked us all, and then took us into the KP Dom two by two. It was all supervised at the time by a man whose name was Koroman. And after searching us, when they finished searching us, they took us into a room which was dark. We were all exhausted and in a state of shock, but we tried -- groping, we managed to locate some beds there, and we went to sleep on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the first name of Koroman?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At a later time, did you become aware of where he worked before, before you arrived at the KP Dom or before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: When talking to other detainees, I learnt that he used to be -- that he was a former warden of the KP Dom in Foca. I mean, before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, this individual is referred to in the guard list, P3, number 32.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Koroman supervised, basically, your arrival. Did he supervise what was going on, on the outside of the KP Dom, the frisking that you mentioned; or was it just the activities that were occurring on the inside?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: He was both in front and inside the building at the time; that is, he was present when they searched us outside, and he was also present inside when they were taking us in two by two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say that you were searched on the outside, were you searched by soldiers or civilians or police? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: It was dark and I really cannot recall, but I think they were guards because I recognised some of the men afterwards, later on during my Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. stay in the KP Dom, and they were all guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went -- when you were placed in your room that night, were there other people in the room as your group arrived?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: No, not in that room. We were the only ones, that is, the 22 of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the building that you went to, went into, or the room number?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I do, yes. It was Room 20.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you detained at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I spent some 13 months there, if you mean the period of time I spent in the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the date that you left?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: It was I think on the 18th of June or July, I'm not sure. I left for Rudo on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which year is that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the first night you stayed in Room 20. How long did you stay in Room 20 for over that 12-month period, 12- or 13-month period?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I spent most of or the bulk of the time in Room 20, I think more than one-half of my detention in KP Dom altogether. But I also spent some time in other rooms, and I was there for different periods of time. I could not really tell you exactly when it was that I was moved from one room to the other, but I spent most of my detention there in Room 20.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the KP Dom, were there many other Muslims also detained?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes. There were other Muslims, too, but they were in other rooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any Serb detainees at the KP Dom when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes, there were also some Serb detainees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they kept separately from the Muslims, or together?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: They were kept separately from the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to your room, the room that you stayed in, where were they kept?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: For a while, they were kept across Room 20. I cannot remember the number of their room, but I think it was 21.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say across from Room 20, was that on the same level as Room 20?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes, it was on the same floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you arrived, how many Serb prisoners were there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I could not really say how many when I arrived because we were locked up and we had no information, nor were we able to get any information. Besides, we were in a state of shock. We were not really interested in surroundings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Other than the room that you slept in, were you allowed to move about the camp freely?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: In the early months we were allowed only -- to leave the room only when we were going out for meals, and we had three meals a day. Towards the end of my stay in the KP Dom, however, we were allowed to walk around for one hour a day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were the guards stationed in relation to your room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: The guards were all over the compound practically, but they also had a small room at the entrance into -- well, let me call it pavilion number 2, where they had their office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the camp, who appeared to be running it, a civilian authority or a military authority?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Those were civilian authorities, if by this we mean the police forces, civilian police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever told why you were detained at the KP Dom for the year that you were there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: No, I was never told. I wanted to know why, and I wrote a number of statements, a number of requests to the warden asking to be interviewed, but I was never received by anyone, I was never interviewed, and I never learned why I had been detained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you start writing a request to the warden for an interview when you first arrived or at some later time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: No, not straight away. It was after a while. Because some people began to be taken in for interviews, and I expected that my turn would come. And when I realised that almost everybody had been to interviews except me, then I wanted to write a request, a plea to the warden to ask him to see me and he explained to me why I had been detained. People who were with me said that it would be a good idea and told me that the prison warden was -- the camp warden was Krnojelac. Later on in communicating with guards, there was a guard who also advised me to do so - his last name was Milic - and he told me too that I could write a request, address it to Warden Krnojelac, and that he would see that he gets my request. And that is what I did, but I never received any reply. And after that I did the same, I think five times all together, but there was never any reply and I finally realised that nothing would come of it and I gave up writing these.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you start writing your requests? Was it after your fellow detainees told you that Krnojelac was warden or was it after you were told this by the guard?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I first learned it from other people, from detainees, that the warden's name was Krnojelac. But then when I talked to guard Milic, he merely confirmed it and said that I should address my request, my submission, to Warden Krnojelac, and that is what I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember Milic's first name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think he could have been Milorad or Milisav. They sound a bit alike. But I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his age, approximately, and can you give a brief description of him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Well, at that time he could have been slightly over 30, I think, of medium height, and he was losing hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe this person to be number 23 on the guard list, P3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is that the only description you've got of him?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I can try for a bit more, Your Honour, but in relation to the list, there's only one that appears with those details. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What, slightly over 30, of medium height, and losing his hair?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the surname. And the Christian name is similar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the colour of his hair?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I do, yes. He was fair-haired, very fair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you arrived at the KP Dom on the 25th of May, 1992. About how long after you arrived did you write the request? About how many weeks?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it could have been approximately four to six weeks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you get the writing material to make this written request?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Well, KP Dom was a professional penitentiary in Foca before the war. We found there full lockers of the former prisoners, and there were all sorts of things there: pencils and ballpoints and books and papers. So that is how we could write, because we had what to write with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you give this request to the same guard each time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was Mr. Milic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And about what time difference, what time elapsed between your separate requests? How long did you wait before you wrote a new one?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Well, about seven to ten days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were your requests ever successful? Did you ever get to speak to the wardens, to Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get a reason from Milic as to why you weren't getting a meeting with him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: No, I was never given a reason why he was refusing to see me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the KP Dom, how much did you weigh?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: About 100 kilograms, like now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you left the KP Dom, had you lost weight or had you remained the same weight?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I had lost 46 kilogrammes when I came in Rudo, or rather when I left the camp in Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the camp did you feel that you received sufficient food?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: This is not really an issue, is it? The issue, as I understand it, is simply that everybody in the area was starving. That's a matter which the Prosecution has faced up to in relation to other witnesses. But there is no dispute that there was very little food for the Muslim prisoners. If he can give evidence that the Serb prisoners, if there were anybody there still, got more food, that would be relevant, because I understand that to be disputed. But the fact that these prisoners had very little food has not been disputed in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'll get to that topic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Serb prisoners get the same amount of food as the Muslim prisoners? Can you say?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: No. They were getting enough food. They had a special kitchen and special food was being prepared for them. And they also could receive visits from their relatives, and they brought them food too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever punished for trying to get more food?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes, several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: On one occasion a friend of mine and I tried to carry a garbage container, because every time we left our rooms we tried to seize every opportunity to find some food. So we started carrying this container to a particular place in the KP Dom. But there was another garbage container which had previously been in the room where Serb detainees were being kept, and that container was full of remains of food that they had discarded. But for us, it was proper food. And we collected these remains of food from the Serb container, if I may call it that, and after that we were beaten and taken into isolation cells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was this friend of yours that tried to get the food as well?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: It was Dzevad Cosovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get the food and eat it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes, we did manage to get some food from there and we did eat it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was it discovered that you had taken the food?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: That garbage container was empty the previous day, and my friend Cosovic thought it might be a good idea to fill it with some other refuse from the room so that we could ask the guard the next day to allow us to take out that container with garbage. And so we filled this container with bits of paper and all sorts of other garbage. We simply tried to make it look full. And we were granted a leave to take this container out. However, the two guards who were changing -- who were on duty then, they remembered that that container had been emptied the day before, and then they realised what we had done. And that was why the head of shift that day, and his name was, if I can remember well, Zulka, Zulka, he used to -- he was a karate man. I can't -- his full name eludes me right now, but he took us out, and in the morning, perhaps around 6.00, and in the corridor in front of the isolation cells, he started beating us. And when he finished beating us, he locked us up in an isolation cell. I remember now, his name was Zoran Matovic, Zulka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anyone else present when you were being beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes, another guard was present. His name, his last name was Obrenovic, but he did not beat us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he do whilst you were being beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: He watched.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the beating that you received?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: We had got up. We had hardly woken up, so to speak. As soon as we got into the hall near the isolation cells, Zoran Matovic started hitting us with karate blows. First he hit me a few times. I tried to protect my head with my arms and hands. Then he moved on to my colleague Cosovic, and then he was hitting both me and Cosovic with his hands and kicking us with his feet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was beaten more severely, yourself or Cosovic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Cosovic was beaten more severely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any injuries from this beating?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes. I got bruises in the head and also in the stomach area. In Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the stomach area, actually, it was not bruises but pain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did Cosovic receive any injuries?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes, also the area of the head and of the back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this beating, I think you said that you were placed in the isolation cell?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes. We were both taken to the isolation cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long, for how long were you placed in the isolation cell?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I think we were not there long. As far as I can remember specifically, I never spent the night in the isolation cell. The same day the head of the guards, or whoever, would come. At that time it was Savo Todovic. I remember. He came to inspect the new people who were brought to the isolation cell, and he asked everyone the same question, why they were in the isolation cell. He came in the afternoon on that day, and we said to him why we were there. He cursed us and said that we should go to Room 20.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Zoran Matovic tell you why he was beating you? I mean, you explained the reason you felt why he was, but did he state it to you directly?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes, he did. The reason was what I had already explained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other occasions when you were -- were there any other occasions that you were beaten for trying to get extra food?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Personally, I was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you witness anyone else being beaten for trying to get extra food?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I did not have an opportunity of seeing that. For the most time I was locked up in the room, so I didn't really have the opportunity of seeing much. I was in the isolation cell several times because of food, though. Like on the previous occasion, I would invariably get out on the same day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were you placed in the cell because of food?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Well, when we would go to the canteen for lunch or dinner, we were exhausted and starved. We tried to get an extra slice. We resorted to different devices in order to get that extra slice because that meant life to us. When they would catch us getting this extra slice, then they would send us off to the isolation cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many times were you placed in the cell for trying to get an extra slice of bread?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Approximately three times, together with the first case that I explained earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for these other two cases, for about how long were you placed in the cell?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I personally got out on the same day every time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on these two occasions, do you remember who placed you in the cell for trying to get an extra slice of bread?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I remember on one occasion that a guard nicknamed Mara took me. That's how he was known. I don't know whether his last name was Maric or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, in relation to the previous incident with Zoran Matovic and the guard Obrenovic, Zoran Matovic appears at number 48 on the guard list, Obrenovic appears at number 46 on the guard list, and the incident referred to is in the indictment at paragraph 5.20 and also in the schedule at A5 and A9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst you were in detention, did you meet an (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes, I met (redacted). We were together in the room. We spent a lot of time together in Room 20.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you witness an incident in which he was beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes. I had the opportunity of seeing two incidents when he was beaten up. Once when we were coming back from the canteen, when we were going back to our room, number 20 - Room 21 I think was open where Serb detainees were - they put a table there on purpose, and they put lots of bread on it. It was a trap for us Muslims to come in and get some bread, which (redacted) did. When he entered in order to get some bread, Serb detainees rushed to him from various corners and started beating him. They actually beat him up. We intervened with the guards, very loudly. The guard came and resolved the situation; however, (redacted) was beaten up, and he came back to the room, and later on he was all black and blue. On one occasion, I remember that (redacted) was beaten up while he was standing in queue at the canteen. We were not in the same room at the time. I was watching from the window from Room 20 or 23, I can't remember. The detainees would have to queue two -- queue up two by two, and then they would all go to canteen together. As they were waiting for everyone to get there, a soldier came up in a uniform, and he started beating not only (redacted) who was in the first row - he was the first person in the first row - but also several others who were in the front rows. I remember that then the guards were very excited. After that, they talked about it and said that everything ended well compared to what it could have been like. Those are the two things related to the beating of (redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that he was beaten up whilst he was standing in the queue at the canteen, and you said that you saw this from your window. Was this in the prison yard, or was this in the building, in the canteen within the building?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: No. That happened within the compound in front of the canteen while people were waiting for everyone to get there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the soldier that beat this person up?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: No, I can't. This was quite far away from the place where I was. And we didn't even dare watch because we were forbidden actually from looking out of the window then. I can only say that it was a soldier because he wore a military uniform, a camouflage military uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And about how many guards were present when this beating was occurring?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I think that in fact one guard was present, the one who was on duty while people gather there to go. However, there were many guards who did various things within the compound. At that moment there might have been two guards who were present there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that you saw this incident, and you've also said that you were forbidden from looking out the window. Did you see it, or did you hear about it, or did you just see it for a short, a very short period of time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I saw it very briefly. Later, when (redacted) came to my room, when we were together, when we talked, then he confirmed this to me as we talked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: [redacted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: [redacted] [redacted].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, that incident that was referred to by the witness relates to -- we believe it relates to 5.12, paragraph 5.12 in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of the incident where a prisoner attempted to escape from the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that incident. This was towards the end of my stay at the KP Dom Foca. It was the very end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want you to discuss the incident in any great length, but do you remember the name of the prisoner that tried to escape?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I remember his nickname, because I was never in the same room with him. He was in a room where the so-called working groups were, groups that worked all the time. But I can assume that that is the name under 216 on the list that I have in front of me. I can tell you his nickname. The nickname I know. I know him by that nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, he's referred to the person on the Exhibit 408. That person and the person above -- this sheet isn't as accurate as it should be -- are in fact not protected witnesses either, but perhaps we'll just continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you lectured about this incident by someone from the KP Dom, about the escape?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes. After that they took the entire KP Dom out to a plateau within the compound, within the prison compound. Then Savo Todovic lectured us. He took (redacted) out. That was the name of the person who had tried to escape. And this is what he said to us: "(redacted)," he said his name and surname. I have forgotten it right now, "has tried to escape. However, he did not succeed. We did not kill him for that, and in this way we showed all the humaneness of the Serb people." That is what he said verbatim. I remember that. However, afterwards he said, "However, now you will all be punished, absolutely everyone. Your food portions will be reduced." So instead of the food that we got, which was horrible in the first place, then we got literally three spoonfuls only. Also, I know that working groups, entire working groups, were punished by solitary confinement for dozens of days. I also remember that perhaps a few days later, five or six days later - I can't remember exactly - during the next five or six days I remember that we really got three spoonfuls only per meal. However, I was fortunate to have left the KP Dom. After that I went to Rudo. I don't know how long this punishment lasted, because I stayed in Rudo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst you were at KP Dom, did anyone require some urgent medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes. There were many such cases. I remember the first case. That was just after the detainees from Herceg-Novi came, specifically the group from Herceg-Novi. A detainee came with me. I can only remember his first name. It was Enes. He had problems with a stomach ulcer from earlier on. Probably since he was in a state of shock his condition deteriorated. In the evening, around 8.00, he started vomiting blood. From the window we called out to the guard to come and help, because we realised that the situation was serious. The guard came to the door. I remember it was Jovan Savic, nicknamed Jovo, who asked what the problem was. When we explained what it was, he only closed the door and left. We thought that some kind of help would arrive, but none did. The next day, around noon, again we sought intervention. The man was half dead. They told us to carry him, and four of us did. We put him on a blanket and four of us carried him out to the yard, where the ambulance from the hospital was waiting, and they took him to the Foca hospital. We heard that he died the same day and that he was buried there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you first complained to the guard, Jovo Savic, you said that he just left the room. Did he say anything at all?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: No, he didn't say anything. I can remember that he closed the door rather cheekily and perhaps he swore at us too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long was the problem explained to him that this person was vomiting?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Very brief. He just stood at the door. When he found out why we were calling him, he was not interested. He swore at us and slammed the door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Enes? Do you know where he was taken?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: As I already said, we carried him out to the yard, to the gate, where a hospital ambulance was waiting. We just put him into the ambulance. I could not see, but we had assumed that they were taking him to hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear whether he lived or died after this?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: We heard that he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, this incident is referred to as 5.37 in the indictment, and Jovo Savic is number 55 on the guard list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were arrested with an Enes Bico.

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you last see him? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I last saw him when they told him to get ready, that he was going out for an exchange. I remember that when we were saying goodbye, he said, "Today it's exactly 100 days that I've been in the camp." According to my math, it should be around the 10th of September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's in 1992?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he said he was going for an exchange, did other people go with him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: He went in a group with around 18 men. However, these people were taken from different rooms. From Room 20, where we were right then, about six or seven people left. I can't remember exactly. But we knew, as we were watching through the windows surreptitiously, that about 18 people left in that group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Enes in your room or in another room when he was taken out?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: He was in my room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Enes Bico ever return to the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: No, he never returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since that date do you know of anyone that knows whether he has been seen alive?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: We do not know of him ever having been seen alive again.

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: (redacted), although Enes Bico was registered when the International Red Cross first came to the KP Dom Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other 17 that were in the group, did you know any of their names that were taken out on the same day?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I can remember only one more name of a person who was also in my room. This was a youngish man. And I was in contact with him. I probably remember the name. It was Karovic. Actually, his last name was Karovic. Aziz. I'm not sure whether Aziz is his first name. No, Ramiz. Ramiz is his first name, not Azim. Ramiz Karovic. I'm sure now. His brother and father were also in the camp. However, we were not all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have probably another 20 minutes of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's all right. I just want to sign one of these redaction forms before I go, to catch it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Shall I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no. No. But if I don't sign it now, it will be broadcast without the redaction being made. The timing of these things is rather important. We'll adjourn now until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, with some of the names that will be mentioned from now on, if you can not state how you know these particular people, but just state whether you know them. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the break you said that Enes Bico was taken from the KP Dom for exchange and to the best of your knowledge you know of no one that has seen him alive since that date. Does the same apply to Ramiz Karovic, who you also stated left on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the other 16 that were taken out in the group, do you know whether any of those 16 have been seen alive today by anyone, have been seen alive since that day by anyone?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honours, because the witness said he did not know those other people, that he only knew one of them, or rather two from that group, that he did not know any others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Where did he say that, though?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for His Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Where did he say that, Mr. Bakrac, that he only knew two of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before the break he was asked by my learned friend and said that 18 individuals had been taken out. And then my learned friend asked him which ones of them he knew, and he said that he knew Bico and also quoted that other name; that is, he said that he knew those two from that whole group. This should mean that he does not know all the others in that group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not sure that is accurate. What he said was: "I can remember only one more name of a person, who was also in my room. That was a youngish man," and he gave a name. But are we dealing with people he knew or whose names he knew? That's the point, as I understand it. He didn't say he didn't know them; he could only remember the names of two.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite so, that he could remember only one other man, that he did not remember others, that he did not know who else was in the group. So how can he now identify others and say whether others from that group were seen later on or not if he does not remember them, regardless of whether he knows them or not? He simply does not remember who those others were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'll only repeat it this time. He said he did not remember their names. He does not say he does not remember who they were, and the Prosecutor is entitled to attempt to find out, with assistance, if necessary, who they were. Now, you proceed, Mr. Smith, but he has said he only remembered two names, so you'll have to go about it some other way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, since this date that Enes Bico went missing, did you make some inquiries as to his whereabouts? Did you talk to other people about trying to locate him, without saying who you spoke to specifically?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: While I was in detention, I of course had no opportunity of learning anything about Enes Bico. We all thought that he had been exchanged and was in a free territory. But when I came out of the camp and realised that Bico has never turned up in any free territory and that he had not been exchanged, then, together with his other relations - his wife, his mother, his sister - we all tried to find out what had happened to him. Of course, they were making those efforts even while I was in the camp, but they never were able to trace him and could not find anything about him. We, which is worse, do not know whether he is dead or alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But during those inquiries, did you speak to other people about the whereabouts of the other 16 that were taken out that same day or did you learn any information about their whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes. After I came out of the prison, we, the veteran inmates, to call us so, we communicated and tried to exchange information and learned about each other, so that I found out that the group which left on that day, that none of those men had ever been seen again or found anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Does that clear the matter up, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, yes, but I think that what Mr. Bakrac was concerned about was that you were going to start by leading questions, going through each of the 18 in the group. If you want to go to any of the others, you have to remember the witness does not remember their names, so you'll have to somehow have some other description.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I think that will be enough for this topic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The following people - Senad Krdalija, Mirsad Borovac, and Alija Cardalkija - were they detainees at the KP Dom? Please don't state how you know these particular people, but can you say whether they were detainees whilst you were at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes. Those men were brought together with me but the names are not quite correct. Alija Cardalkija was one of them, Sanin Krdalija was another one, and Mirsad Borovac. These are the names of those men. They were brought together with me from (redacted) and they were with me in the KP Dom for a while until they were taken away, and to this day we do not know what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present when they were taken away or did you hear this from other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I could look through their window on the sly - we usually did that whenever there were so-called exchanges of groups -- and I therefore saw when Sanin Krdalija was taken away and I also saw when Mirsad Borovac was taken away. I did not see, however, Alija Cardalkija being taken away, but I heard that same day from other detainees about him, because he was in the first pavilion and I was in pavilion 2 at the time when he was taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst you were at the KP Dom were you ever asked to pick plums?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this, about?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: It was -- it could have been in September or perhaps early October. I couldn't really be quite precise in my answer. But I remember that a guard came in. His name was Vukovic. And he entered Room 20 and lined us up and then asked, "Any volunteers to pick plums?" We all wanted to go pick plums, because at that time a plum really meant something to us. And he began to take down the names of volunteers. So a couple of men volunteered and he took their names. And then another guard came to the door, rather small and dark, with dark complexion, whose nickname was Predo and who said that he should stop taking those names because he should go back to the command urgently. And he did that, and about perhaps half an hour or an hour later - I cannot tell you exactly - Vukovic came back and simply read out the names of men who should go and pick plums. No. Excuse me. It was not Vukovic; it was Plevaljcic, Vlado Plevaljcic who came. He read out the names of men who were to go plum picking, and I -- it sticks still in my memory that he read out the name of a young man, of a very -- of a young boy. He could have been 18 or 19 and had been wounded in the arm. He had a cast on that arm and practically could not use it. And he told Vlado Plevaljcic that he could not go to pick plums because he simply was not up to it. But Vlado Plevaljcic said then, "Well, you come downstairs, see what it's like, and if you don't like it, then you can come back." And so the group went and that young man never came back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can just stop you there. About how many people from your room were selected for that group?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: About ten, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether people from other rooms were also selected?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes, and there were men picked out from other rooms. And as far as I can remember, of course, from other detainees who were better informed than I was, some 36 men were -- had been taken away to pick plums.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the names of any individuals that were taken out of your room?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I do, yes. I remember engineer Murat Crneta. I also remember a big man whose surname was Murto. Then I also remember a man whose nickname I know, and that was Zeka. Before the war he worked in the Foca hospital, in the military department.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they take their belongings from the room or did they leave them behind?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: No, they did not take their belongings with them, because they had been told that they were going to pick plums and would be coming back, unlike other groups, which had been told, "Get your belongings ready. You've got about half an hour and you're off to be exchanged."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to their belongings?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Their belongings stayed there for days and we could already hear rumours that those men had been liquidated. So after a while we began to use those things, because we needed them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of those people that you knew in the group, do you know of anyone that has seen them alive since that time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: As far as I know, nobody saw any one of those men who had gone to pick plums alive again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you stayed at the KP Dom for about 12 months and then you were taken to Rudo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay at Rudo for?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Some nine months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Rudo? Was it a detention camp or was it some other facility? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: We were taken to Rudo so as to be exchanged for prisoners captured by the BH army in Gorazde, captured on the Rudo theatre of war. So we were brought to Rudo and we were put in the cellar of the cultural centre. I mean, it was proper, a proper cellar. There were some small windows with bars, but no window panes. And we were told that we would be kept there for three or five days, that the exchange had been agreed, and that we were simply waiting for some technical details to be resolved. However, the exchange did not take place and we stayed nine months there. Now, was that a camp or something else, well, I suppose you can make your own conclusions. There were about 30 to 35 people locked up there in a cellar. No hygienic facilities, no sanitary conditions. I don't know what you would care to call that. Those men were civilians, by and large, picked from their homes, brought from other states.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were these people Muslims that were detained at this place?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Only Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after the nine months you were taken to the KP Dom at Kula in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you stay at this camp?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Five months or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And about how many other people were detained there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: There were many people, because people were being brought and taken away. I know that the cells were overcrowded. There were military bunk-beds in those cells. I couldn't really give you the number, but there were several hundred men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just by way of comparison, the conditions that existed at the Rudo detention camp, were they better or worse than that in Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: In Rudo the conditions were better because people who were guarding us there, Serb guards there, were incomparably more humane than those who guarded us in Foca. I can just give you an example. When 30 or so of us arrived in Rudo and when those Serb guards saw us, then their comments were like this, and they were loud comments so we could hear: "What had those Chetniks in Foca done do you? Fuck them." And because we were completely emaciated. People in Rudo gave us better food and in quantities which were normal. They also allowed us to come out of that cellar and do something if we wanted to, and of course we did want to, because it's not very pleasant to stay in a cellar. So we did all sorts of things, all sorts of chores, but nobody forced us to do them. And we all gained at least 25 kilogrammes while in Rudo during those nine months.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what date you were released from the Kula camp in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: It was the 17th of August, 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Red Cross visit you whilst you were at the Foca KP Dom and Rudo and at the Sarajevo KP Dom at Kula?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes. The Red Cross came to see us in the Foca KP Dom, but only after we had been there for five or six months. In Rudo they came to see us regularly, and at Kula they also came to see us regularly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you obtain a certificate from the Red Cross referring to those visits and your detention at these places once you were released?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I was issued a certificate by the UNHCR, that is; a certificate as to the camps I had been kept in and the time of my release.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you also subsequently receive a certificate from the authorities, the police station commander at (redacted), in relation to your arrest and detention and transfer to KP Dom after you were released?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: My wife has such a document, and it happened shortly after my arrest, seven or eight days, because she was persistent. She kept going there, asking why I had been arrested, where, and the man could not explain anything to her, but he could issue her a certificate that I had been arrested at the instructions, at the order of the Montenegrin government, and that I had been turned over to the Serb authorities in Foca. And the same certificate was issued to Bico's wife, to Enes Bico's wife. His fate is unknown to this day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also, without stating the content of the inquiries or who made the inquiries, but are you aware of inquiries made with the Red Cross in relation to Enes Bico and the subsequent results that they gave? But I don't want you to refer to which Red Cross or who made those inquiries. Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes, an investigation was started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And subsequently did you receive some paperwork in relation to his whereabouts from the Red Cross? If you can just give a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this paperwork was provided to the Tribunal by yourself or someone, a relative of yours?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Enes Bico's wife sent me the documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You've actually used it yourself occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I apologise, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender Prosecution identification number document 81, which is a Red Cross certificate relating to this witness; also identification number 83, which is the certificate in relation to -- from the authorities in relation to his detention and transfer to the KP Dom, and the translation, and it's for this witness and Enes Bico; and also an answer to a tracing request in relation to Enes Bico, which is a document from the Red Cross, identification number 76.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have you got copies of all of these? They're not easy to find.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You can have these copies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have you got copies for everybody?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Everyone has been given them in the folders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You have never, obviously, had to look through those folders for documents by number. It is almost impossible. You have to turn over every page, practically, to find the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'll remember that for the next occasion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, your colleagues always manage to produce copies of them, and it is, if I may say so, the better way of dealing with it. Well, Mr. Bakrac, have you been able to identify these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, we did, and we have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, have any of these got to be under seal? 81 would.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: All of them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And 83 would.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And there's a further one, Your Honour, that would also require to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
