utterances.text: Which one is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Because I've just handed over the documents, Your Honour, I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: There's three, three documents there that relate to -- three documents that relate to -- no, it's just the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's what I would have thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. Then we'll -- they will be become Exhibits P75 and 76, and then P81 and 83, the latter two being under seal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Witness, one last question. You spent a year at the KP Dom. Can you state how that affected you mentally after leaving and how it affects you today?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I don't know what to say from the point of view of mental health. I can tell you how it affected me physically. I had lost a terrible lot of weight. I even got some illnesses, like a hernia. I was sick many times. I went to see a doctor very often, or rather this male nurse called Gojko. I don't know what I would say about my mental health. I can say that everything that happened was abnormal. I mean, I could not understand that something like that could be happening in this century. I can't understand that until this very day, that people in the twentieth century can starve to death, and there were such cases, that people hate each other so much, I mean really hate. It's not that they don't give them something, that they don't give them food or -- it's not that they cannot give them food; they don't want to give them food. There was an abundance of food. We saw food being thrown away and we were in a situation to starve to death, just because it occurred to someone to divide people according to ethnic groups. I think this was insane.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Cross-examination? Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Vasic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to wish the witness a good day and to introduce myself. I'm Miroslav Vasic and I am one of the Defence counsel for the accused, Milorad Krnojelac. Sir, did you give statements to the investigators of the OTP on two occasions concerning your stay at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give these statements on the 2nd of December, 1998, and the other one on the 9th and 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact dates, but it could be that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. After these statements were typed out, did you read them and sign them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, the one you gave to the investigators of the Tribunal in December 1998, did you mention the following: "Savo Todovic was in charge of logistics in the KP Dom"?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I probably said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please let me finish the quotation, if that isn't a problem for you.

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: All right

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "However, people talked about him as the real commander of the KP Dom. He behaved in a harsh way. He lectured us, and once he made one group go to the isolation cell." Is that what you said to the investigator?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Did you say to the investigator of the OTP that Mr. Savo Todovic was present when, on the 13th of June, 1993, you were transferred to Rudo from the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I think I stated that. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: It is correct. He was present, as well as many others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, did you state to the investigator of the Prosecution that from the very beginning of your detention you would see soldiers in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I can't remember whether I stated that. We saw soldiers very seldom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to read what it says in your statement dated December 1998: "I saw soldiers at the KP Dom from the very beginning of my detention."

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Perhaps I meant the guards at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll read it to the end and then you'll see that there is a distinction.

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "They came to the administrative building, but I could not see what was going on there. I never saw the soldiers enter detention cells, but I heard that it was the soldiers who treated the detainees the worst." That is the quotation that I wanted to draw your attention to, so there is a clear distinction between guards and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: That is correct. I mean, what you read out is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. In relation to the army, I would like to draw your attention to yet another thing you stated in your statement to the investigators of the OTP: "While I was staying at the KP Dom, I noticed that the soldiers Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were the worst. They would come and take people out. The soldiers ordered the guards to bring people to them, and the guards obeyed them. I don't know what the soldiers did to these people, because we did not have such information." Is that what you stated? Or rather, is this correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I did state that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: When I stated that, perhaps at that moment I did not know who a soldier was and who a guard was, because many guards did not wear uniforms; they wore civilian clothes. And very often they wore camouflage military uniforms as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, in your statement to the investigators of the OTP, did you say that during your stay in the KP Dom Foca, did you say you did not see Milorad Krnojelac a single time and that you did not know who he was?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. In your statement today you said that after you came to the KP Dom Foca after being transported, you were frisked and you were taken to a room where it was dark. Can you explain to us why it was dark in that room? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Because at that time there was no electricity in Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Today you stated that in your opinion the KP Dom in Foca was run by a civilian authority.

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to what you've said to us about the military, on the basis of what do you think that the civilian authorities ran the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Because Warden Krnojelac himself was a civilian, because in that prison, to the best of my knowledge, there were guards who had also worked as guards in the KP Dom before the war as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You said that you gave Milic requests in writing for the warden to receive you. Do you know whether these were actually taken to the warden?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: He personally claimed to have taken them to the warden.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You stated today that Serbs who were detained at the KP Dom had special food and a special kitchen. Can you tell us who cooked for them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: It changed from one period to another, but I think that for the most part Serbs cooked for them, headed by the chief cook, whose name was Risto, I think. There were periods when Muslims helped out, but it was primarily for the Muslims that the Muslims did the cooking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know what these Serbs ate, specifically? Do you know what was cooked for them? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I did see that. I had the opportunity of seeing that. This was food -- for example, if it were beans, we would get beans where we could see literally three kidney beans swimming about, where there was no meat, not any kind of fat whatsoever. We could drink it as if it were water. Whereas the Serb detainees would get beans that had lots of beans in them and meat and everything. There was a drastic difference. It was the regular kind of beans you would eat in normal life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You are the third witness that has appeared before this Court during these past few days, and you are the first one to mention the throwing away of food into a container. Can you explain to me why you did not mention this fact to the investigators of the OTP although you talked to them twice, although you discussed the question of food as well, although you gave your statement to the best of your recollection and to the best of your ability, as it says in the statement? Why did you not mention, in a single word, this fact?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I was simply ashamed to talk about that. I simply didn't want to remember that. I wanted to erase that from my memory. Because when I got out of the camp and when I went to (redacted), doctors, psychiatrists, asked me whether I needed help, and I said, "No. I want to help myself." That was probably one of the ways in which I tried to help myself, to forget the worst that happened. And also these conversations were exhausting, they lasted all day, and I simply wanted to forget them as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Tell me, though: In such a situation, is it now that you recalled these things? I mean, how come you remember that now?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I simply knew that all the time. I did not think it would be important. I did not know that I would be a witness in this Tribunal. However, at this moment I realise that this is an important thing that I should state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did somebody tell you that this is an important thing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: No, nobody told me. I thought about it. When I decided to testify before the Tribunal, I decided what I should say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I agree, sir, but when you gave a statement to the investigator of the Tribunal, you also said that if necessary you would come and testify here as a witness.

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: That's quite possible. However, what I stated about the food is a pure fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that a detainee named Enes got sick and that you carried him to an ambulance with three other detainees.

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who were these other three men who carried him with you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I can remember one name. It was Sefko Kubat. I cannot remember the other two names. Sefko Kubat also died in prison in Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when this was, this event with him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: This was at the very beginning, when we had just arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, when you are giving the answers to Mr. Vasic, you should keep in mind that you are both speaking the same language. The interpreters have to catch up with the question, so would you please pause before you start the answer, just sufficient time for the translators to catch up. They're usually about a half sentence behind. Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From who did you hear that the person named Enes had died in hospital?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I heard that from the others who were with me in the room, who knew him well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us a name of one of these persons?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I remember Sefko Kubat. He was a very good friend of his.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you how come he knew?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: He did not tell me how come he knew, but in the Foca camp most of the people were locals from Foca, and they got news from somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Today you gave us details related to an incident when you were beaten up. Can you tell us -- this was together with Mr. Cosovic. Can you tell us where you were taken from when you were beaten up afterwards?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: We were taken out of Room 20. We were woken up in the morning and we were taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Today you mentioned that you know that Mr. Krdalija and Mr. Borovac were taken away. Can you tell us when this was, if you can remember the date, month, or year?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I can't remember the date exactly, but it was in 1992. Mirsad Borovac was taken with a big group which was allegedly taken out for an exchange. These were two buses full of people. One of these buses did arrive in the so-called free territory, in Roze, in Montenegro, whereas the other bus never arrived anywhere. The people who were in that bus have not been heard of until the present day. Mirsad Borovac was in that bus as well. Sanin Krdalija was taken with a group, similar to Enes Bico. I can't remember the exact date, but in the period of August/September many people were taken, in my estimate about 400 people, most of them young. People were usually told that they would be exchanged, except when they went out to pick plums. However, when I got out and when I talked to the survivors of the camp, we came to the conclusion that nothing is known about most of these persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me which room Mr. Krdalija was taken out of and which room Mr. Borovac was taken out of?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: There were many rooms in the prison. Many times they put us together or separated us. It was so often that I could not remember which rooms they were taken out of at that very moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Today you mentioned the events related to plum picking and calling out names in that respect. In response to my learned colleague's question, you added that you remember that one young man had a cast on his arm. Is this the first time you mentioned this? Have you told the OTP investigators about this?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: This is the first time that I mention this. I remember certain things, but I don't know many names. That is why I tried to find out this young man's name and surname, because I was really affected by this. I realise that the man who was calling out people's names knew exactly where he was taking them, and he nevertheless called out the name of this young man. However, I didn't manage to find out what his name was, but I decided to talk about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is why you did not mention this incident, because you did not manage to find out what the person's name was?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I do think that the translators deserve a medal for that one. You were very quick off the mark, Mr. Vasic. Please do pause as well, would you?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honour. I got carried away in my examination, obviously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, was that the reason why you did not tell the investigators of the OTP about this detail, although you discussed this subject and although this subject is part of your signed statement?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I don't know what the reason was why I did not say this to the investigators. However, I can only say that this is a fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Today you said that you heard that a group which went to pick plums was liquidated. Who did you hear this from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I heard about this from the other detainees who were with me. I repeat again: Most of them were local people from Foca who knew each other well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me one name, one name of one of the persons who told you about this?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Well, they all talked about it. Literally everyone talked about it. I can mention ten names, if necessary: (redacted) (redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. Could you please pay attention to this list with pseudonyms so that you wouldn't -- I mean, if you're going to mention any people from this list, please bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: All right. Everybody knew, number 214, 66, 82.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you how come they found out that this group was liquidated?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: At that time there were two working groups. These were the so-called metal workers and the carpenters. Also, there were groups that went out to work from time to time. These groups could find out a lot when they went out, and they did find that out from the outside when they heard, accidentally, conversations among Serb soldiers or civilians, and then they would tell somebody about it, and all news spread through the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you're talking about rumours, and it was not ascertained as to whether they were true or not. But you're talking about rumours that spread through the KP Dom, am I correct? I mean, I'm not claiming this or that.

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: It is not for me to say whether these are rumours or not. The fact remains that none of these people have ever appeared since. Can you give me an answer where these people are?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I said -- without any intention of claiming whether this is true or not, I just tried at this moment to find a common denominator in terms of what you have just told us about. Thank you very much. The Defence has no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Your Honour. Reexamined by Mr. Smith:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you were asked a question by my learned friend in relation to your knowledge of Mr. Krnojelac from a statement you gave the OTP. In your answer you said that, "In my statement, I said that I didn't meet Mr. Krnojelac, nor did I know who he was." In your examination-in-chief, you stated that when you arrived at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the KP Dom, other detainees advised you that Mr. Krnojelac was the warden, and then later Mr. Milic, a guard there, also told you that he was the warden, and subsequently you wrote written requests to Mr. Krnojelac for a meeting. If I can have the -- is that correct? Did you not know who Mr. Krnojelac was? Is that what is written in your statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Has he got the document in front of him?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps I'll do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't want there to be some problem about translations here. There was no objection at the time that Mr. Vasic read that part out, so I assumed that it was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I was going to raise it in re-exam. That was the approach that I took.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think it would have been easier for the witness to have -- I'm not sure which version you're going to give him, the English or the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The B/C/S version, Your Honour. I understand the difficulties, but it's 74A.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in that statement at paragraph number six, do you see paragraph number six where it mentions Mr. Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You state that you wrote a letter to Krnojelac and that other detainees told you that you should write the letter to him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you gave this statement, did you know whether Mr. Krnojelac was the warden or not?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: I knew that Mr. Krnojelac was the warden, but I had never seen him, and I did not know him before the war, nor did I have an opportunity to see him in the -- within the compound because I was locked all the time. But I did know that he was the warden, and it was confirmed to me by a guard whose last name was Milic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, would you be able to recognise Mr. Krnojelac whilst you were at the KP Dom? Did you know what he looked like when you were at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: No, I did not know what he looked like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned that the soldiers you felt treated the detainees worse than the guards, in answer to a question by my friend.

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: Yes. It was based on rumours that reached me. Specifically, I had no opportunity of seeing the soldiers treat the prisoners except once briefly when I saw them beating number 214 and others who were queuing for meat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the guards enjoy a good reputation in terms of treatment of prisoners, or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: FWS-8
utterances.text: There were all sorts of things there. There were guards who, especially in the beginning treated prisoners, very decently, but their number was very limited. The majority of guards treated prisoners very cruelly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I have no further questions, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for giving evidence. You're now free to leave, but if you'd just wait a moment until the blinds have been pulled down so that you may leave the courtroom without the public seeing you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There's no change in the particular provision for the next witness is there, Ms. Kuo?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: No, there isn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you got a pseudonym sheet for this witness that we can have a look at?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Yes, we have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration on the card that's being shown to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please. The document headed FWS-142 will be Exhibit P408.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it's 409.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you're right, 409, and it will be under seal. When you're ready, thank you, Ms. Kuo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour Examined by Ms. Kuo:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have been given certain protective measures in this case, including the use of a pseudonym rather than your real name. Do you understand that? You need to say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll ask you to look at the sheet of paper in front of you, and on that sheet of paper, which is Prosecution Exhibit P409, you'll see FWS-142. Underneath that, is that your name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Beneath your name, is that your birth date?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And throughout the course of the trial, you will be referred to by that number. Now, Witness, in April of 1992, what town did you live in?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What part of Foca did you live in?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: The centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you live with? Don't give us their names, but what their relationship to you were.

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: My family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does that include your wife?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any children?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they live with you as well?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What ethnicity are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in April of 1992, what kind of work did you do?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: I was in a non-production sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the war -- when did the war in Foca start?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: The war started on the 8th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: In the morning hours, fire started, individual shots could be heard, but it grew into -- it escalated into bursts of fire, and after that it was followed by heavy artillery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to work that day?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: I was at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay at home?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: I was there till I was arrested on the 13th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that time when you stayed in your home, did any soldiers come to your building?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: They did on the 15th of April, at the time when they were clearing, cleansing up that part of the town of people of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell us what the soldiers did when they came to your building?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Well, they ordered that all people of Muslim ethnicity should come out of the building and cross the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Then they singled out men, and some 20, 22 of them. They handcuffed them and took them away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you among the men that they selected out?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was in the beginning, but when they took that first group, they let me go and, I think, another three men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why you were not taken away, even though you were selected?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the men were taken that day who were taken away?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Well, I learned that they had been taken to so-called Livade. There was some warehouse there or some hangars, and that is where they took them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you learn that they were taken there since you yourself were not taken?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: They took there a man whose wife worked for a trading company, and she was a good friend of Dragan Causevic, called Coso, who had taken that group away, so that through his father she interceded, managed to get him back, and she learned from him that they had been taken there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you remember the identities of some of the men who were taken away that day?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us their names?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Murat Crneta, Munib Veiz, Zulfo Veiz. That's all I can remember now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see those three men again at some point?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: I saw them after I was brought to the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: For the Court's reference, Munib Veiz is in Schedule C, 28, and Zulfo Veiz is C 29.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the people who took away these Muslim men, could you describe who they were, what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Dragan Causevic, called Coso, was there; Kovac, the one who was here in The Hague, his brother; and there were some outsiders, some volunteer guards from Serbia Montenegro, but that was the patch that they had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they in military uniform?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were they Serb?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you described that you were arrested on the 13th of May, 1992. Can you tell us how you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: I was taken away from my friend. I was sitting at home with two neighbours when two men came to look for a neighbour, one of those who was sitting with me. They took him away, and after a short while they came back and to take me, too, allegedly. They had the order to take me to the KP Dom so that I could make a statement there. And whilst we were in the flat, they also made me write a statement as to what I was doing, where had I been, had I attended some meetings, been on guard somewhere, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The two men who came to take you, were they dressed in military uniform?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The neighbour of yours whom they took away, was he Muslim or Serb?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were with another neighbour as well. Was that neighbour taken away?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What ethnicity was he?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The statement that you were asked to make in -- while you were in your flat, do you know what happened to that? Did you have to sign it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: I signed it, but what happened to the statement, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were told -- what was the reason you were given for being taken to KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: They said that they only knew they had to take me to the KP Dom so that I could make a statement, and that I would be back the next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they complain about the statement you made so that you would have to make another statement at KP Dom, or was there any mention of why you would have to make another statement?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at KP Dom, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Well, they took me to the main gate, and there at the reception, Milan Vukovic took down our names and particulars. And at the gate after Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the search, the guard took us into the compound, and there in front of the canteen, Mitar -- there was Mitar Rasevic standing there who said "hello" to us. And the guard asked where to take us, and he answered, "Well, how about 18, any room there?" And that one confirmed it, so that we were taken to Room 18.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you kept in Room 18?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: In Room 18 we were until about early May 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you put into a different room after that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which room were you put into then?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Fourteen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you kept in any other rooms while you were at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which ones?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Room 15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was the warden at KP Dom while you were there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: According to information, Mr. Milorad Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the information on which you base that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: A detainee was taken down to the gate, to that administrative building, and after a while when he came back to the room, he said he had seen Warden Krnojelac because he had been visited by his fellow workers there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the guards ever refer to Milorad Krnojelac as the warden?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Later on guards talked, because there were some prisoners who wanted to speak to him, and they were saying that one had to write a written application and submit it to the warden.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know of detainees who were able to meet with the warden?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: This was the only instance I knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Krnojelac from before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Well, I knew him because he was a townsman in Foca, he was a teacher there, but we were not close or anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Krnojelac while you were at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often would you see him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Two or three times, maybe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On those occasions, what was he doing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Twice I saw him walk across the yard to the canteen, and once while we were lined up in the yard of the compound, he was sitting on a bench.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what he was wearing, civilian or military clothes?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: On that occasion when he was sitting on the bench, he had a military uniform on him. And on those two other occasions when he was moving around, he -- perhaps he was in civilian on one of those occasions, but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he doing when he was sitting on the bench; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Yes. It was when a prisoner had tried to escape, and they nevertheless caught up with him and brought him back to the KP Dom. Then they were taken out one room after the other, and Savo Todovic was there taking us to task all the time while the Warden Krnojelac just sat there. He did not say anything. And Savo Todovic was saying, "See how we caught this gentleman who tried to escape. You see," he said, "the sound [as interpreted]. Nobody has harmed him, which is just another proof how correct is the army of Republika Srpska." And he insisted that he did not do it on his own but that somebody was using him as a test.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While this was happening, was the Warden Krnojelac in a position to listen and to see all of this?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever speak with Mr. Krnojelac at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, while you were at KP Dom, were any detainees beaten that you know of?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell us the names of these detainees and what you know happened to them.

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: On one occasion, Hasan Dzano, and Emir, Enes were taken down to the gate, and when they came back they were so badly beaten that they could hardly move. And Mandzo was even barefoot; that is, he had his shoes in his hands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: I think it could have been somewhere around mid-June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of what year?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who beat them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say they were taken to the gate, what gate are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: The gate which led from the compound into the administrative building. It is a metal door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of anyone else who was beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: In late June 1992 things got worse than ever. At that time I think 40 to 45 men were taken away. They would be taken away around dinner time in groups of about four or five. And I remember when they were down at the gate, I said [as interpreted], Kisovac [phoen], Nisic, Nurko Nisic, and Husko Rikalo, I think, because there were three Rikalo brothers, and they would take them into the compound. And as soon as they got them there, we could hear immediately screams and shouts, which meant that the beating had started. And I heard a voice moaning, moaning, until there was any strength left, and at that moment I also heard a male voice yelling, "Nurko, do you know what happened to Bota?" And then I also heard a shot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that, did you hear anything else?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: The sounds of a car, a car, the engine being switched on in front of the building, because either the exhaust pipe had fallen off or something, but it was very loud when it was switched on. And it left, and after a while that car came back again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: I'm afraid it's 1.00, so we need to take our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now until 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Kuo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness mentioned Emir Mandzo, and he is listed as incident number 37 on schedule B. And Hasan Dzano is listed in schedule B at number 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, before the lunch break you were describing hearing the sound of a car. Do you know what kind of car it was specifically?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: I think it was a Zastava Kedi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you heard the car that night, did you ever see Nurko Nisic or Husko Rikalo again?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, Nurko Nisic, the incident where he is beaten is described in the indictment at paragraph 5.27, and Husko Rikalo is listed in schedule C at 21, as well as on schedule B at 46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other -- just going back to the same incident, you said you heard somebody say something about Bota. Can you -- do you know what that was in reference to?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Later on we received information that allegedly he ran into a mine with his vehicle and that he remained disabled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if that person, Bota, was a Serb or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear other people being beaten at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe that for us, who and when?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Aziz Sahinovic was beaten by guard Jovan Savic. After the beating he was in isolation cell for about two weeks, up to 20 days, actually. He told me about this in December, when he came to our room, because the night before he was taken away, in December, the guard, Savic, came to the door, again called out Sahinovic's name. He probably thought that he was being taken to a beating again. He went all white, as if there weren't a drop of blood in his face. However, he was only transferred to another room with six or seven more prisoners, and they spent the night there, the 11th, 12th December, between 6.00 and 6.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when Sahinovic was beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: I think this was the month of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other people who were beaten, whom you actually heard being beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Halim Konjo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was beaten at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Yes. I omitted to mention that. Halim Konjo, Bico Salem, Granov Adil, and Selimovic, nicknamed Spona, were among the first to be taken out. When we were returning from lunch, I heard moans and screams downstairs. I think that it was Halim Konjo's voice, and not a single one of them ever returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when that was, what date, or approximately?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: I think this was the beginning of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember where the sounds you heard were coming from, what building or rooms?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Down there from where the administration was. On the ground floor there were some rooms. I don't know exactly what.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, the people who were mentioned by this witness, Halim Konjo is listed at schedule C, 13; Adil Granov, schedule C, 9; and Salem Bico, schedule C, 2. And Mr. Bico is also mentioned in the indictment at paragraph 5.27. In addition, the previous person mentioned, Aziz Sahinovic, is mentioned in the indictment, paragraph 5.29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know a Dzemo Balic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to him at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: When I was detained on that 13th of May, 1992, the prisoners in the room talked that day, said that they had beaten him up and locked him up in an isolation cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The others in the room said who had beaten him up?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he returned to that room at some point, the room where you were in?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: I think he was returned about a month later to the same room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see what condition he was in when he was brought back?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: I could not notice anything, because after all, a period of one month's time is long, but he said that he was beaten up badly. And that's precisely what they did. When somebody was beaten up real bad, then they would lock him up in an isolation cell and keep him there until there was no trace of it on him any longer and then they would return him to the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Dzemo Balic's father's name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is a Balic, first name unknown, listed at schedule B, number 4, as the son of Serif. And we're not sure if this is the same person, but we bring it to your attention.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there people whose injuries you did see, injuries from being beaten?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: I saw Vahida Dzemo's and Delic's too. I can't remember what his first name was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see on Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: During the day he was taken to the gate, and then about half an hour later he was returned to the room. There were obvious injuries on his head, in the area of his nose, and on his lips. He said that they took him into a cell, that all of them were his neighbours, and that they only put a tarpaulin over him and that they all started beating him. One of them even said, "Let's see if you're going to come and hunt game near my house again."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he mention whether the neighbours were civilians or in a military uniform? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: He didn't say anything about that. He just said that they were neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: There is a Delic mentioned in schedule B at number 14.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know and could you tell us what happened to Vahida Dzemo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: As for Dzemo Vahida, I saw his injuries and bruises in the area of his eye when he went for lunch before he came to the room, to my room. He spent some time in my room, and in mid-September he was taken away with a group of the so-called plum pickers. They were taken out to pick plums.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Mr. Vahida is mentioned at schedule C, 27, and also in the indictment at paragraph 5.29.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Salko Mandzo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: On one occasion he was taken down to the gate. After about 20 minutes to half an hour he was simply pushed in through this metal door, returned into the compound, and he had a bandage on the left-hand side, somewhere around his chin or neck, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this? Do you remember the approximate date?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What had happened to him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Later on we found out that allegedly he was called out by mistake. It wasn't him they were looking for. They were looking for Fudo Mandzo. And indeed, after he was returned, sometime after that, Fudo Mandzo was taken to the gate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to Fudo Mandzo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: As he was taken out then, he never returned again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Fudo Mandzo, Your Honours, is listed in schedule C at number 16, and the incident regarding Salko Mandzo is listed as paragraph 5.28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have to work while you were at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of work did you do?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Well, I did a bit of work around the compound, and then in September a group was established of some 20 men, and we went to the mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of work did you have to do in the mine?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: We went into the pit. We loaded the coal that we mined. We took that coal out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you volunteer to do that work or were you forced to?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: I was forced to. One day when I was in the compound, I was cleaning beans, and Mr. Savo Todovic came to ask me whether I would work in the mine. And I said that that was not really for me, that I was exhausted, that I had no strength, that that was hard for me. He answered, "Well, there is nothing for us to discuss really." And then either before lunch or after lunch, a guard came, Vlatko Plevaljcic, and read out a list of some 20 men who were assigned to go work in the mine and that they were supposed to report the next morning at the gate at 6.30.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned that you started to work in the mine in September. What year was that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: 1992, the 19th of September, 1992. Sorry. Sorry. 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you finally released from KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: On the 16th of August, 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were the circumstances of your release?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: I went to be exchanged at the Bratstvo-Jedinstvo Bridge. However, on that day, the exchange did not succeed. We were returned to Kula, we spent the night there, and then the next day we were taken out to the Bratstvo-Jedinstvo Bridge again and were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your whole time at KP Dom, were you ever charged with having committed a crime?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever told why you were held there, even after you gave your statement?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: No. In the KP Dom I never gave any kind of statement at the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So even though you were told you were brought there to give a statement, you were never actually asked to make a statement at KP Dom; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: No, never. Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result of your detention at the KP Dom, how did you suffer physically?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Well, I was exhausted, starving. I had lost a lot of weight. My feet would swell a bit when I worked in the mine, and I had pain in my back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you suffer emotionally or psychologically?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: I was there. I was powerless. I thought I would never get out of there, especially because they kept us hidden from the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Those are all the questions from the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Cross-examination. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Bakrac:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I would like to introduce myself to you. I am Mihajlo Bakrac, attorney at law, one of the Defence counsel for the accused Krnojelac. Is it correct that you made statements, both to the investigators of the OTP, as well as at the centre of security in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you gave one statement on the 25th of June, 1996 to the investigators of the OTP and the other one on the 22nd of October, 1998?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the statement you gave to the Sarajevo Security Station was on the 14th? No. Sorry. On the 23rd of August, 1994?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Most probably. I don't know the exact date, but I did give a statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you agree with me when I say that in the statement that you gave to the security station in Sarajevo, you pointed out that Savo Todovic, who was otherwise in charge of us Muslims and for work assignments, is it correct that a person named Savo Todovic was the person who was in charge of assigning people to work and that according to your own statement he was in charge of us Muslims?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Well, listen. In the compound he was the one who directly gave orders to the detainees and who said things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to read a sentence from one of your statements, the one that I hope you are not denying that you signed, the one that you made to the Sarajevo Security Station: "A day before, I went to work in Rudo."

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: The mine. That's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, yes, it is a mistake: "Savo Todovic, who is otherwise in charge of us Muslims and for assigning people to work asked me whether I would go to work in the Branko [phoen] mine in Miljevina."

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Exactly. That's what he asked us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you stated this?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: He was in charge of the entire compound within the compound. The Muslims and the Serbs. He yelled at them just like he yelled at us. And now, whether he made these lists on his own or whether he got these lists from someone else or instructions from someone else, that I don't know about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the command and administration chain in the KP Dom or are these your assumptions?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: At the beginning of my testimony I said that a prisoner who went to the administration building and came back to my room said literally that he went to see Warden Krnojelac, because that was his colleague from work, when he had a visitor, that is, and also later. Whoever was supposed to go see the warden, Krnojelac, the guards would say that a request in writing should be addressed to Krnojelac, the warden, in name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So those are all the circumstances and facts that led you to such a conclusion or did you know anything else in greater detail?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: That is all I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you stated that you saw Savo Todovic wearing a military uniform, that you saw him walking around the prison compound, and that you saw the guards in the prison compound talking to him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that in the statements given to the investigators of the OTP, you pointed out that until the outbreak of the war conflict, you had not noticed that Milorad Krnojelac, before the outbreak of the war conflict, was politically active?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today you said that it seems to you that you saw Krnojelac twice in a jacket, in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Once in civilian clothes. Will you agree with me that in your statement to the OTP you said that from time to time he wore civilian clothes and from time to time he wore a uniform and that you did not remember that he carried any weapons?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: I agree as far as weapons are concerned. As for uniforms, I think, I think, I saw him once in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also correct that you decidedly stated to the investigators of the OTP that you had never seen Milorad Krnojelac in the rooms where the prisoners were held, nor did you ever see him in the KP Dom at night.

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know whether your answer was audible, but please speak up.

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I had not seen him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of all the facts that we covered and what you observed and concluded about Savo Todovic, and in view that you heard that Krnojelac was a warden, only from the source that you already told us about, could you then really acquire a proper picture of his jurisdiction in the KP Dom, about his terms of reference there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Whose terms of reference?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac's.

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: The very word "warden" -- as I said, Savo Todovic was the man who communicated with us, Muslims and Serbs alike. Now, I repeat: Whether he did it on his own or whether he had orders to do, that is something that I do not know. But the warden, the warden, I think, is about everybody else. That's what I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that a large number of witnesses, that is, more than 50 per cent of those who have testified so far before the Tribunal, used words such as that Krnojelac was a warden de jure, not de facto, that he was a warden on paper, that his opinion did not really carry much weight? Did you come by such information when talking to other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Don't answer it yet, please. What's the relevance of that? He can't comment upon what other people have said. You may make that comment at the end of the trial. We're interested in what this witness can say. We're not interested in what this witness has to comment about what other witnesses have said. Is that the point that you're arising to make, Ms. Kuo?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. It really -- I mean, Mr. Vasic asked a similar question of a witness, but not in quite such extravagant terms, this morning, and I should have stopped that one, but please do not ask witnesses to comment upon the evidence given by others. It is of no assistance to us at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my apologies. Perhaps I did not word it properly or perhaps I was not understood properly. My learned friend asks the witness and the witness answers about certain things that he heard from other prisoners, and I wanted to ask the witness whether, in his conversations and comments with other detainees, he had ever heard such a definition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: A number of witnesses have said that the guards, to use a neutral term, have described your client as the warden. A number of witnesses have said that they have heard other people who were inside the KP Dom as saying that your client was the warden. You could ask that. But you have asked far more than that. You have used the expressions that they have given when giving their evidence. You are asking him to comment upon the evidence they've given. Now, a witness may here have said in his statement, as I think he agreed, that he used those appalling Latin terms Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. "de jure" and "de facto." A lot of people believe that's bad Latin, but that's another matter. That is what he said in his statement, not that he had heard another person inside the gaol say that, but that was his description of your client's position in the KP Dom. So you are really asking him to comment upon their evidence. Now, if you want to ask him specifically how did he hear other inmates describe your client, by all means ask that. That would be a permissible question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. That was what I intended to do, and I probably simply misphrased my question. What I wanted to ask the witness was whether he had heard other detainees make such comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think you became a little over enthusiastic about it, Mr. Bakrac, so let's go back and start again. Now, you ask him a question along those lines, and there should be no objection to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear other detainees comment the terms of reference of the Warden Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: We did not hear any comments about Warden Krnojelac, but we were surprised to see Todovic communicate with us directly of some people to various tasks, put people in solitary confinement, and that's that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us a while ago about your work in the Miljevna mine, and you said that you were sent to work that in September 1993. Was your group the first one to go to work in Miljevina? Would you know that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that in your statements, which I listed to you before, you said that you had Gojko Jokanovic, a nurse in the KP Dom, who visited you daily, and that twice a week Drs. Vladicic and Dobrilovic also came to the penitentiary?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not sure that people could hear an answer.

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said -- or rather, no, what I'm asking is, did you say in your statements that in the kitchen it was Krsto Krnojelac and somebody called Raso were the cooks in the kitchen, and my question is, did they also prepare food for you, for the detained Muslims?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Well, they were the chief -- they were the bosses there. The food was prepared by Muslim detainees, and they were there simply to supervise them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the KP Dom when you arrived there, did you find there Serb inmates serving there their terms following the judgement pronounced upon them before the war?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of, what kind of judgements those were, but yes, there were a couple of such inmates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this principle of cooking which you've just mentioned, did it apply to them, too?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who prepared food for them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Well, the cooks. They had special food. They had better food, more wholesome food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was those same cooks that we've mentioned who prepared their food?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: No, no, no, no. Not the Muslims, but Krsto and Raso.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever put in solitary confinement -- did anyone beat you while you were at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A while ago you mentioned an incident where after some beating you heard a vehicle and you said it was Lada -- it was a Lada Kedi. Does a Lada Kedi have an engine which is different from the engine of a Zastava 101?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: No, the engine is the same. It is merely the, the car which is different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how could you say that it wasn't a Zastava 101 but a Lada Kedi?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Well, I could do that because metal workers who came from the metal workshop, they talked in the morning that it was a Kedi, and they had washed it because it had bloodstains.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did they know whence the blood and where that vehicle had come from?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: Well, it used to happen after those -- in the end of June, as I said, after beatings, when 40, 45 men were taken out in smaller groups, and they worked in that metal shop and washed that car. Because that car wouldn't stay there more than -- stay away more than ten minutes and it would be back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the only car? Was that the only car which they washed?

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: That morning that was the only one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking about other days.

utterances.speaker: FWS-142
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. I suppose as the need arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir, for giving evidence. You may now leave, but would you wait whilst the blinds are lowered so you may leave the Court without being seen by the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The next witness has been waiting a long time to give evidence, I gather. Her name has been on the list for some time. No particular measures are required?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it is Ms. Manas. Your Honour, while we're waiting for Ms. Manas to come in, I just want to tell you the following. We have -- just this morning we have filed the list of witnesses for next week, but during this break, the lunch break, I was informed that the Witness 47 on this list could not be reached by the Witness Unit. It seems to be that he is in hospital or, at least, under medical treatment somewhere, so this witness will not come. We are trying to replace him with the witness 144. This witness could come, but it is still not sure that the travel arrangements can be made in time. This is for you to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much, then, for the Defence to be forewarned. Is the other witness ready to come in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Please take the solemn oath. I'm sorry, solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Please sit down, madam. Examined by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Manas.

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Manas, would you state your name, profession, and your position in the Prosecutor's Office?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: My name is Racine Manas. I'm a criminal investigator for the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And since when do you work in the Prosecutor's Office?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: I've been working in the Prosecutor's Office since April 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do before you came to work in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Prior to my work with the Office of the Prosecutor, I was employed as a criminal investigator for the South African Police Services since January 1983. I investigated all kinds of crimes, chiefly sexual abuses and murders. My last office that I worked in I investigated mostly political violent crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the year 1996, did you visit Foca?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes. We visited Foca on the -- June, June 16th to 18th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the purpose of this visit?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: The purpose was -- of the visit was to visit various detention facilities in order to make photographs and videos and forensic testing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which particular places did you document? Did you have -- already decided upon that?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We have various places that are documented. There were Partizan Sports Hall, the KP Dom, the military complexes of Buk Bijela, Velecevo prison complex, the Motel and Hotel Zelengora, the Aladza mosque area, and the Foca High School, and there were a number of others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you document the places? What did you actually do?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Photographs were taken and video clips were made, and at some places, especially the KP Dom, forensic testing was done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who assisted you in performing this job?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: The Office of the Prosecutor was assisted by a forensic Dutch expert, Mr. Schouten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his specialisation, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: He was a forensic expert attached to the Tilberg forensic unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you make the photo documentation of Foca that's Exhibit 18 in these proceedings, the photo binder?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. I made it together with Mr. Schouten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you also write a report on your findings?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the exhibit -- this is not yet an exhibit, sorry. This is the document with the ID number 41 in the binder, and it's called "Personal Observation of Crime Scene Investigations As Follows," and then there's actually a description of where the investigators went, including sketches and some findings. We would like to enter this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, what's your attitude to the document going in to evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, that will be Exhibit P41.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Manas, this report that you made, did Mr. Schouten assist you in making this report as well?

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Yes, to a certain extent. While the report I made is based on my notes, personal notes I made on the site, which is in this book, and in the evening I electrically transferred them to those notes which you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Manas, Ms. Thapa has already testified about the various places that were visited on this occasion and, we do not need to repeat this evidence that was already given. I rather would like to ask you a few additional questions to some of the places; especially, would you explain how you organised your report and how it relates to the photo binder.

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Okay. The report refers to the sequence I visited, the different facilities mentioned there, and -- here, I think that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, Ms. Manas has the original photo binder. It's only -- she brought it here because the quality of these photos is much better than the copies that we have. It may be that we have to look for a specific in the original photos.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, would you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, is it in evidence at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, it's Exhibit 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's Exhibit 18, the photo binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I know it was marked for identification 18, but it has become an exhibit, has it? Perhaps the court deputy can help us.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, through, through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Thapa, was it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Ms. Thapa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Manas, in relation to this photo binder, I just would like to know from you how the numbers under the photos relate to the indexes you made.

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: Okay. It consists of 14 parts which is numbered from A to N. Under each part we have a numbering from one to infinity, and so on and so on. In other words, that it's a new set of numbers; it's not a continuation of the numbers. And the index itself refers to the photos themselves under each sections, and the numbers on the right-hand side of the photograph refers to the numbers on the index, and the numbers underneath the photos refers to the evidence reference numbers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Does the photo binder include all photographs you made on this mission to Foca? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: No, not really. Some of the photographs were of a poor quality, and only the photographs that were really relevant, relevant in the aspect -- I mean, that -- discussed by witnesses over their testimonies that were included in this album.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Witness, I just would like to discuss one photo related to Partizan, and it's the photo 7295. To make the process --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers slow down a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Manas, to make it shorter, you can always use these copies and you do not have to look for the original. Ms. Manas, what do you see on this photo? Can you point out the -- it's actually a double.

utterances.speaker: RACINE MANAS
utterances.text: You're missing the other part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
